div.head: Af 42.4
div.ab: Eac swelce, gif mon becume on his gefán, ⁊ he hine ǽr hamfæstne ne wite, gif he wille his wæpen sellan, hine mon gehealde XXX nihta ⁊ hine his freondum gecyðe; gif he ne wille his wæpenu sellan, þonne mot he feohtan on hine. Gif he wille on hond gan ⁊ his wæpenu sellan, ⁊ hwa ofer ðæt on him feohte, gielde swa wer swa wunde swa he gewyrce, ⁊ wite ⁊ hæbbe his mæg forworht.

..tne ne wite, gif he wille h...pen sellan, hine ....ehealde XXX nihta ⁊ hine ... freondum ..cyþe; ..yf h...ll.., his wæpenu ...llan, þonne mot he feohtan on hine. Gif he wille on hond gan ⁊ his wæpenu sellan, ...him feohte, ... swa wunde ...wyrce, ⁊ wite ...æg forworh..

Eac swylce, gif mon becyme on his gefán, ⁊ he hine ær hamfæstne ne wite, gif he wille his wæpen syllan, hine mon gehealde XXX nihta ⁊ hine his freondum gecyðe; (⁊) gif he nelle his wæpen sellan, ðonne mot he feohtan on hine. Gif he wille on hond gán ⁊ his wæpen sellan ⁊ gif hwa ofer ðæt on hine feohte, gylde swa wer swa wundwite, swa ðær he gewyrce, ⁊ wite ðæt he hæbbe his mæg forworht.

Si quis etiam superueniat in hostem suum, et eum antea residentem nesciat, si hostis ille uelit arma sua reddere, custodiatur XXX noctibus et amicis suis offeratur. Si nolit arma sua reddere, tunc licet eum impugnare. Si uelit in manus ire et arma sua reddere, et aliquis super hoc impugnet eum, soluat sic weram sic uulnus sicut egerit, et witam et perdat quod de cognatione sua requirebat.

Eac swelce, gif mon becume on his gefán, ⁊ he hine ǽr hamfæstne ne wite, gif he wille his wæpen sellan, hine mon gehealde XXX nihta ⁊ hine his freondum gecyðe; gif he ne wille his wæpenu sellan, þonne mot he feohtan on hine. Gif he wille on hond gan ⁊ his wæpenu sellan, ⁊ hwa ofer ðæt on him feohte, gielde swa wer swa wunde swa he gewyrce, ⁊ wite ⁊ hæbbe his mæg forworht.

Eac swelce, gif mon becume on his gefán, ⁊ he hine ǽr hamfæstne ne wite, gif he wille his wæpen sellan, hine mon gehealde XXX nihta ⁊ hine his freondum gecyðe; gif he ne wille his wæpenu sellan, þonne mot he feohtan on hine. Gif he wille on hand gan ⁊ his wæpenu sellan, ⁊ hwa ofer ðæt on him feohte, gielde swa wer swa wunde swa he gewryce, ⁊ wite, ⁊ hæbbe his mæg forworht.

Ebenso auch, wenn jemand auf seinen Feind trifft, welchen er bisher nicht als sesshaft kennt, vorausgesetzt, dieser wolle seine Waffen ausliefern: so bewahre er ihn 30 Nächte und melde ihn seinen Freunden. Wenn jener seine Waffen nicht abliefern will, dann darf er gegen ihn fechten. — Wenn er [der Verfolgte] sich unterwerfen und seine Waffen abgeben will, und einer trotzdem gegen ihn ficht, so gelte dieser [Rächer] so Wergeld wie Wundbusse, je nachdem er [Todtschlag oder Verletzung] verübt, und Strafgeld, und habe [den Entgelt für] seinen Verwandten [den er rächen wollte] verwirkt.

Likewise also, if someone comes upon his enemy whom he did not previously know to be settled at home, provided the latter is willing to hand over his weapons: then let him keep him 30 nights and announce him to his friends. If the latter will not hand over his weapons, then he may fight against him. — If he [the pursued man] is willing to surrender and give up his weapons, and anyone nevertheless fights against him, let that [avenger] pay wergeld or wound-compensation according to what he does [killing or injury], and a fine, and let him have forfeited [the payment for] his kinsman [whom he wished to avenge].

And further, if anyone chances on his enemy, not having known him to be at home, and if he will give up his weapons, he shall be detained for thirty days, and his friends shall be informed [of his position]. If he is not willing to give up his weapons, then violence may be used against him. If he is willing to surrender and hand over his weapons, and anyone after that uses violence against him [the pursuer], he shall pay any sum which he incurs, whether wergeld or compensation for wounds, as well as a fine, and his kinsman shall forfeit his claim to protection as a result of his action.

Likewise, if a man run across his opponent, and did not previously know him to be at home, if he will give up his weapons, he is to be kept for 30 days and his friends informed; if he will not give up his weapons, then he may fight against him. If he is willing to surrender, and to give up his weapons, and after that anyone fights against him, he [who does] is to pay wergild or compensation for wounds according to what he has done, and a fine, and is to have forfeited [the right to avenge] his kinsman.

Similarly, if a man comes upon his enemy, and he did not know before that he was in his house, if he [the enemy] wishes to give up his weapons, let him be held for thirty nights and let his friend-group be notified. If he is not willing to give up his weapons then [the accuser] may attack him. If he [the enemy] wishes to turn himself in and give up his weapons, and someone attacks him despite that, let [the attacker] pay such wer as is due for wounding [he has caused], and a fine, and he has forfeited his kin-compensation.

Das Folgende benutzt aus Q Hn 83, 3; vgl. Gl Blutrache 14
Hn 83, 3 uses what follows, from Q; cf. Gl Blutrache 14

nicht ‘beibringt’; s. o. 7, 1. — In folg. Z. meint Q vielleicht, obwohl frei übertragend, richtig: ‘was [Räch]er von seiner [des Totschlägers] Sippe beanspruchte’, denn deutlich versteht er in Hn 83, 3: quidquid adversus eum [den Totschläger] habebat forisfaciat. Auch Lambardes Umschreibung trifft wahrscheinlich Af’s Sinn: eaque parte omni quae sibi cognationis nomine debetur excidito. Erst Wilkins missversteht völlig: facultates suas perdet, als sagte Af mægen. Spätere erklären: ‘Rächer verliere seine Magenschaft’ [als stände mægðe oder Plural da], nämlich werde aus der Sippe gestossen. Und dies wegen einer zugunsten dieser getanen gefahrbringenden Bluttat?! Wie wer erst ‘Mann’, dann ‘Wergeld’ bed., so ist hier der Sinn von mæg entwickelt zu ‘dem den erschlagenen Verwandten büssenden Geldanspruch’

not ‘inflicts’; see above 7, 1. — In the following line Q, though translating freely, perhaps correctly means: ‘what the [aveng]er claimed from his [the slayer’s] kindred’, for in Hn 83, 3 he clearly understands: quidquid adversus eum [the slayer] habebat forisfaciat. Lambarde’s paraphrase too probably hits Af’s sense: eaque parte omni quae sibi cognationis nomine debetur excidito. It is Wilkins who first misunderstands completely: facultates suas perdet, as if Af said mægen. Later writers explain: ‘the avenger shall lose his kinship’ [as if mægðe or a plural stood there], i.e. shall be expelled from the kindred. And this on account of a perilous act of bloodshed committed on its behalf?! Just as wer means first ‘man’, then ‘wergild’, so here the sense of mæg has developed into ‘the monetary claim compensating for the slain kinsman’

[Setze diese Zahl über ‘Wundbusse’] ‘Wundenstrafe, wie er da verübt, und wisse, dass er habe’ verderbt H. Er verkennt Af’s wite ‘Strafe’ nächster Zeile als ‘wisse’ und bildet ein sonst nicht vorkommendes Kompositum ‘Wundenstrafe’, während Af dort nur ‘Busse an den Verwundeten’ meint. — Zur Konstruktion vgl. Wülfing Syntax II 162

[Set this number over ‘Wundbusse’] ‘wound-penalty, such as he committed there, and know that he have’ H, corruptly. He mistakes Af’s wite ‘penalty’ in the next line for ‘know’ and forms a compound ‘wound-penalty’ that does not occur elsewhere, whereas Af there means only ‘compensation to the wounded man’. — On the construction cf. Wülfing Syntax II 162

note.label: hæbbe
note.seg: ⁊ wite ðæt he hæbbe etc. H.

I understand hwa (⁊ hwa ofer ðæt etc.) to refer to a third person, a relative of the man who has surrendered. Liebermann takes the sentence differently, understanding on him, as against the man who surrenders, while as subject of gielde, hæbbe he understands the pursuer, whom he regards as exacting vengeance for a kinsman not previously mentioned. Quadr. reads Si uelit in manus ire et arma sua reddere, et aliquis super hoc impugnet eum, soluat sic weram sic uulnus sicut egerit, et witam et perdat quod de cognatione sua requirebat.
i.e. the man who has surrendered his weapons.
Lit. ‘and (thereby) he shall have brought about his kinsman’s undoing.’
